description: A small evergreen tree 6-10 m tall with a dense crown, glossy pinnate leaves with 4-6 pairs of leaflets (young leaves hang limp and reddish), and dense clusters of fragrant orange-yellow flowers that turn red. Fruits are flat dark pods.
cultural_significance: Sacred in Hindu, Buddhist and Jain traditions: associated with Sita in the Ashoka Vatika of the Ramayana, and with Buddha's birth in Lumbini. 'Ashoka' means 'without sorrow'. Not a Vedic-era plant by name with certainty; prominent in the epics and later Nighantus.
habitat: Moist evergreen forests and shaded streamsides of the Western Ghats and parts of eastern India; widely planted in temple gardens and avenues.

uses.title: Women's reproductive health
uses.detail: Bark is the classical herb for Stri-roga: it is described as Garbhashaya-shodhana and used in excessive menstrual bleeding (Asrigdara) and menstrual disorders.

uses.title: Bleeding piles
uses.detail: Flowers and bark are traditionally used as a decoction in bleeding piles because of their astringent, Raktastambhaka nature.

uses.title: Skin and blood conditions
uses.detail: Bark decoction is traditionally given in skin diseases and as a blood purifier.

uses.title: Uterine tonic research
uses.detail: Studies on bark extracts report effects on uterine muscle and anti-inflammatory activity; clinical evidence is limited.

preparations.name: Ashoka bark kwatha (decoction)
preparations.method: Boil bark in water and reduce; strain before use.
preparations.note: Used in menstrual complaints under practitioner guidance.

preparations.name: Ashokarishta
preparations.method: A classical fermented tonic made from bark and other herbs.
preparations.note: Contains self-generated alcohol; common women's health formulation.

preparations.name: Ashoka ghrita
preparations.method: Medicated ghee prepared with bark decoction.

precautions: Avoid during pregnancy unless advised by a practitioner because of its uterine action. Women with heavy or abnormal bleeding need medical evaluation and should not self-treat. May interact with blood-thinning drugs. Many market samples are adulterated or substituted (for example with Polyalthia longifolia, the 'false Ashoka'), so use authentic material only.

cultivation.propagation: Fresh seeds, which lose viability quickly
cultivation.harvest: Bark is collected from mature trees; flowering is in spring

conservation_status: Vulnerable (IUCN) due to habitat loss and bark over-collection.
fun_fact: Ashoka flowers change from orange to red as they age, and the tree is listed among the plants traditionally said to bloom after touch of a maiden's foot ('dohada') in Sanskrit poetry.

regions.name: Western Ghats
regions.note: Native in moist evergreen forest streamsides
